text:
Research documents sensitivity to missing recent interactions, but a deletion-induced accuracy drop alone does not establish excessive recency dependence ([missing-input study](https://iris.uniroma1.it/bitstream/11573/1740238/1/Siciliano_Robust-Training_2024.pdf)). Recommended controls: preserve the last item while perturbing earlier history; separately replace only the last item without changing length; shuffle earlier items while fixing the endpoint and item multiset. These distinguish endpoint identity, earlier-item content, and ordering sensitivity. Compare compacted deletions with position-preserving replacements, treating replacements as a separate intervention: internal padding or unfamiliar tokens can themselves create out-of-distribution inputs. Always read the final nonpadding position in left-padded histories.

For NextItNet, match recent-versus-older deletions within the actual readout’s receptive field; its dilated convolutions impose architectural limits on accessible history ([NextItNet paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163)). Comparing accessible recent items against inaccessible older items confounds recency with reachability. Use paired histories, equal deletion counts and resulting lengths, matched contiguous-versus-scattered edits, fixed endpoint status, and explicit accounting for changed distances and items newly entering the receptive field after compaction. Report unavailable matched comparisons rather than silently changing edit sizes.

Temporal counterfactual research emphasizes minimal edits and preservation of behavioral dependencies ([CETD](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/20/11176)). As a diagnostic design inference, match or stratify edits by training-observed transition support, item frequency, timestamp gaps, and title/description similarity; assess newly joined neighbors after deletion. These are coherence proxies, not observed preferences. Publish seeds, edited indices, eligibility counts, paired validation HR@10 changes and uncertainty; label implausible histories as stress tests rather than causal evidence about user interests.
